job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Welcome, and thanks for sitting down with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in embedded systems, the small computers inside machines like washing machines and car brakes. Mornings I'm in the lab at the university in Harbourside, soldering boards and writing C code, and afternoons I'm applying for jobs from the library. I live with my parents, so I eat Mum's cooking and ride the 7:40 bus. I did the master's because I finished my electrical engineering degree with just a pass and had no internship to show anyone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The sending. I've sent about 60 applications and got three replies, all automatic rejections. Dad, who drives a delivery van, says keep going, but I can feel the gap between what the job ads ask for and what I actually have on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I already expected. The hype is loud and the real change is small. I'd probably post that the companies shouting about it just want investors, and then go back to my soldering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, between us, it means I still have to fight for an ordinary job in a slow market. My pass degree and empty internship line are the problem, not any robot. I'd still worry about the student debt, around 9,000, because the job ads haven't gotten any kinder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's project, a motor controller for a bicycle, and keep applying to small firms around Harbourside. I'd also ask the lab technician, Mr Okafor, whether his old firm takes juniors. I wouldn't touch AI tools, since I don't trust them and don't need them for soldering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly flat, to be honest. A bit relieved that nothing is crashing, but tired too, because the plateau still leaves me with the same stack of rejections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust AI tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lecturer showed us a chatbot writing circuit code, and it invented a component that doesn't exist. If a student did that they'd fail the module. I'd rather make my own mistakes and understand them than hand my judgment to something that sounds sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would be hardest if the job search drags on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan repayments start when the course ends. Mum would help, she's said so, but I hate asking. I'm 24 and my mother still tops up my bus card, and that bothers me more than any robot could.

say: AI is **mostly hype**, and the loudest voices are selling something.
Nothing much changes for people like me, so the **job market** stays as tough as today.
think: My pass degree and **no internship** hurt me more than any machine.
I carry about **9,000 in debt** and feel guilty leaning on my parents.
do: **Finish** the bicycle motor controller project and put it online as proof of skill.
**Apply** to small Harbourside firms and ask Mr Okafor (the lab technician) for a contact.
Keep avoiding AI tools and rely on **hands-on** lab skills.
feel: **Flat** and tired, with a little relief that nothing is collapsing.
S0.quote: I'm 24 and my mother still tops up my bus card, and that bothers me more than any robot could.
fieldNote: Resistant to technology, so he blames **employers** and the market rather than AI.
**Debt** and the missing internship carry the worry here, not machines.
Said the quiet part: being topped up by his mother stings his **pride**.

steps.text: Finish the bicycle motor controller and post it to a portfolio page
Apply to ten small Harbourside electronics firms each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bad deal for new graduates, plain and simple. If software takes over the junior coding and checking jobs, then companies stop hiring the people who need a first step. I'd say we need rules so firms can't just swap every junior for a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my route in is being closed. The easy tasks juniors do, like testing and drawing up simple circuits, are exactly what these tools eat. I never learned to use them and now I feel behind, which is a bad feeling to have at 24.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the graduate section of the engineers' union, which charges about 5 pounds a month for students. I'd stay on the embedded course, since hardware is slower to change. And I'd finally sit through one tutorial on these tools, grudgingly, so I can say I looked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. I'm angry at firms that call it progress while the hiring freeze lands on people my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finally try one of the tools. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Okafor said the testing crew at his old firm all use one, and the ones who refused were let go first. I don't like it, but refusing alone doesn't help if the others have it. I'd do one tutorial and then judge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame most if junior jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms, and the shareholders pushing them. A company that cuts every junior job to save money is eating its own future engineers. I'd want the government to make them train a number of juniors.

say: Firms should be **required** to keep training juniors, not just buy tools.
Graduates need a **union** voice, because we have no power one at a time.
think: My **entry-level** route is shrinking and I'm behind on the tools.
I blame **firms** and shareholders, not the technology itself.
do: **Join** the engineers' union student section for about 5 pounds a month.
Stay on the **embedded** course because hardware changes more slowly.
Sit through **one** AI tool tutorial to judge for myself.
feel: **Angry** at firms, with a quiet fear of being left behind.
S1.quote: A company that cuts every junior job to save money is eating its own future engineers.
fieldNote: His politics gives him a **target**: employers and shareholders, not the tool.
Reluctant move toward AI came from **peer pressure**, not curiosity.
Anxious but still believes **collective action** can help.

steps.text: Join the engineers' union student section and go to the next meeting
Finish the embedded systems master's with a hardware-heavy thesis
Sit through one AI coding tutorial and test it on lab code
Write to the local representative asking for graduate hiring rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a joke. Nobody is ready, not the government, not the university, not my family. I'd say the people running this should be answerable to everyone, and not just the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my whole degree is worth nothing by 2028. I haven't even started working. I'd be one of the last cohort to have studied for a job that no longer exists, and I haven't got any savings or tools to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but food and the loan. I'd ask my parents to let me stay home while I look for any work, even warehouse work, since robots are said to arrive later for hands-on jobs. And I'd join every protest the union organises, because I can't see another lever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, in the stomach. I'd lie awake doing sums on how long 1,200 in savings lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said any work, even warehouse work. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a plan to not sit still. Warehouse jobs are about three more years from robots by that card, so it buys time. I wouldn't be happy, but I'd keep paying my share at home and keep my head above water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents the degree they were so proud of might not be worth the paper, and that I'm sorry for the money. Dad would say it isn't my fault. I'd still feel it was.

say: Two years is **far too fast**; nobody is ready.
The people building this must answer to **everyone**, not only owners.
think: My **degree** will be worthless before I even start.
I have **1,200** saved and no tools to change course.
do: **Cut** everything except food and the loan repayment.
Stay with parents and take **warehouse** work while it lasts.
Join every **union** protest, since I see no other lever.
feel: **Sick** with worry, doing sums at night about how long savings last.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents the degree they were so proud of might not be worth the paper, and that I'm sorry for the money.
fieldNote: His **resistance** to change leaves him no plan except protest and survival.
**Guilt** toward his parents is the emotional centre of the answer.
Thinks hands-on jobs buy **time**, so he would take warehouse work.

steps.text: Cut spending to food, transport and the loan repayment
Apply for warehouse and logistics jobs near Harbourside
Join union protests about graduate job protection
Stay at home with parents and contribute to the bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but I'd say at least there's some time to organise. I'd tell friends we should start pushing for a public plan now, like retraining pay and a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd finish the master's, probably get one junior job before things turn, and then be in the same trouble as everyone else. I'd have maybe two or three working years. That doesn't feel enough to pay off 9,000 and build anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to land a first job in hardware testing within a year, because robots come later for hands-on work. I'd put away 150 a month from the first pay. And I'd learn the basics of one AI tool, mostly so I can tell when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. There's a little hope in having time, but it feels like standing on a train track that's loudly humming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hardware testing in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work is on a bench with real boards, and a person has to plug things in and hold the probe. I can do that even with a pass degree. The paperwork around it will go to software, I guess, but the bench stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the 150 a month be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cushion. I'd rather have six months of rent saved than a clever plan, because a plan needs a job and savings don't. It's boring advice, but it's the only part I trust.

say: Five years gives time to **organise** and push for retraining pay.
We should demand a **public plan** now, before layoffs start.
think: I'd get **one job** and then face the same trouble as everyone.
Two or three **working years** isn't enough to clear my debt.
do: **Aim** for a hardware testing job within a year of finishing.
**Save** 150 a month from the first pay packet.
Learn the **basics** of one AI tool to spot its mistakes.
feel: **Mixed**, with a little hope in having time, but under constant pressure.
S3.quote: I'd rather have six months of rent saved than a clever plan, because a plan needs a job and savings don't.
fieldNote: More strategic here: picks **hands-on** work as his shelter.
Trusts **savings** over plans, a sign of his cautious nature.
Still anxious because his **debt** clock runs shorter than the timeline.

steps.text: Apply for hardware test technician jobs at electronics makers nearby
Put 150 a month into a savings account from the first pay
Learn one AI tool well enough to check its circuit suggestions
Ask the union to campaign for retraining pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds long, and I'd say that out loud, but I'd add that long timelines make governments lazy. We'd need a firm date for a plan, not just another review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the first one where I might actually win. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a decade of experience on real hardware, and I could end up as one of the people who maintain the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and take the first decent job, even if it pays little. I'd build a pension and a deposit fund, and maybe do a part-time course in robotics maintenance at night. And I'd keep supporting the union, since decisions get made by whoever is in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than with the others. It still feels heavy, but I can picture a normal life in there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said long timelines make governments lazy. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my town the council promised a retraining centre when the car-parts factory closed, and four years later it's still a plan on a poster. I trust a date on a calendar more than a promise in a speech. That's why I'd keep pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is calm the same as safe for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Calm means I can get on with life while the problem stays out there. My own money is still thin, and I'd be careful with every pay packet until I felt some real cushion.

say: Ten years is long, but governments need a **firm date** for a plan.
A decade means **robot maintenance** may be a real career.
think: By 34 I could be **experienced** on real hardware and doing fine.
My money stays **thin**, so I'd watch every pay packet.
do: **Take** the first decent engineering job, even at low pay.
Start a **night course** in robotics maintenance.
Build a **deposit** fund and keep backing the union.
feel: **Calmer** than in the other scenarios, though still careful.
S4.quote: I trust a date on a calendar more than a promise in a speech.
fieldNote: **Time** lets his cautious personality work for him instead of against him.
Local example of the closed **factory** shapes his distrust of promises.
Calm but not **secure**: debt and thin savings remain.

steps.text: Accept the first decent engineering job offer, even at entry pay
Enrol in a night course in robotics maintenance
Save for a house deposit and a basic pension
Keep paying union dues and attend local meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, no question. I'd have no time to change my life and I'm someone who needs time. What would help is a guaranteed place to retrain with some pay, and a rule that firms must keep taking juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me aren't lazy or against technology. I'm not scared of machines, I'm scared of being told I'm not needed by a company that never gave me a first chance.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of machines, I'm scared of being told I'm not needed by a company that never gave me a first chance.
portrait: Liam is 24, doing a **master's** in embedded systems after a pass degree and no internships.
He lives with his parents in **Harbourside**, owes about 9,000 and has 1,200 saved.
Progressive and **union-minded**, he blames firms and shareholders more than the technology itself.
Resistant to change: he avoids AI tools, then tries one only because **peers** do.
His mood runs from uneasy to alarmed, with **debt** and pride at the centre.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd have no time to change.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining place** and a rule that firms keep hiring juniors.
